title: Clean and disinfect
summary: Clean with soap and water first, then disinfect with the strong mix or, where food is made, the food mix; never mix bleach with other cleaners, and never drink a bleach mix.

list: Cleaning removes most germs, dirt and impurities from surfaces. Disinfecting kills most germs on surfaces and objects (CDC).
Clean before you disinfect. Wash the surface with soap and water first (CDC). Vomit or stool must be cleaned up before disinfecting, or the disinfectant will not work (CDC).
Disinfect when someone is sick (CDC). Clean things everyone touches often, such as door handles, light switches and counters, regularly (CDC).
Use regular, plain, unscented household bleach of 5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite. Check the label. Don’t use a bleach whose percentage is outside that range or not given (CDC).
Some laundry bleach and splashless bleach are not suitable for disinfecting (CDC). No scented bleach (CDC).
Mix a fresh batch every day. Diluted bleach is not as effective after 24 hours (CDC).
Mix it in a bucket or bottle kept only for bleach, and mark it BLEACH (no source says to mark it). Never put food or drinking water in a container that has held bleach (CDC; see Store water at home).

blocks.warn: These mixes are for surfaces, dishes and laundry. They are far too strong to drink. Never drink them and never use them to treat drinking water: for drinking water, use the drops in Make water safe.

Never mix bleach with ammonia or any other cleaner (CDC). Bleach with ammonia makes toxic chloramine gas; bleach with acids, such as vinegar, toilet bowl cleaners, rust removers and drain cleaners, gives off chlorine gas (Washington State Department of Health). Urine contains ammonia: never pour bleach into a bucket or bag with pee in it.

list: Wear gloves and eye protection, and rubber boots if the job is wet (CDC).
Open windows and doors when you use bleach indoors, and try not to breathe the fumes (CDC).
Read and follow the directions on the bleach label (CDC).

Coughing, shortness of breath, chest pain, wheezing, watery or sore eyes, throat or nose after mixing chemicals are signs of exposure (Washington State Department of Health). If someone has these, use the Poisoning protocol.

blocks.warn: Plain, unscented 5% to 9% bleach and water only (CDC). Never add ammonia, vinegar or any other cleaner, and never pour bleach into a bucket with pee in it (CDC; Washington State Department of Health). Wear gloves and eye protection; open windows (CDC). Mix fresh every day (CDC). These mixes are poison to drink: for drinking water, use Make water safe.

blocks.p: Two mixes do every job in this topic. 1 gallon is 3.8 L; 1 tablespoon is 15 mL.

Besides the container and bucket mixes below, two more special-purpose bleach mixes are each for one job only, and never for drinking water: CDC’s soak for baby feeding items, in Feeding babies and young children, and the National Center for Home Food Preservation’s clean-up mix for a spill from a suspect can or jar, in Food poisoning and botulism (“Getting rid of a suspect can or jar”).

head: Mix
Strong mix: door handles, taps, toilet seats and everything a sick person touches; vomit or diarrhea after cleaning it up
Food mix: dishes, cutlery, cups, and counters where food is made
rows: 1/3 cup (5 tablespoons, 75 mL) of 5% to 9% bleach
Surfaces: at least 1 minute. After vomit or diarrhea: 10 minutes if you can, never less than 5
Dishes: rinse or soak 1 minute. Counters: wipe on and leave wet. Then air dry completely
CDC; New York State Department of Health

blocks.p: CDC allows up to 25 tablespoons per gallon for vomit and diarrhea. This app uses the low end, which CDC’s evacuation-center guidance and the Minnesota Department of Health also use.
Containers for drinking water have their own mix: see Store water at home. Emptied waste buckets: see Toilets when the water is off.

blocks.label: Toilets when the water is off

blocks.warn: If anyone in the group has vomiting or diarrhea, use the strong mix on their toilet seat and on anything they have soiled (worked out from CDC). Their bucket: empty it, wash it with soap and water and rinse it so no pee is left (CDC), then sanitize it as in Toilets when the water is off. Never pour bleach into a bucket or bag that still has pee in it: it makes a toxic gas (Washington State Department of Health).

steps: Wash the surface with soap and water to remove dirt (CDC).
Wipe or spray on the strong mix (table above), or the food mix where food is made.
Keep the surface visibly wet for the whole time in the table (CDC).
Let it air dry (CDC).

blocks.p: Use disposable plates, cups and cutlery if you have them (CDC). Otherwise:

steps: Wash the dishes with dish soap or detergent and rinse them (CDC, New York State Department of Health). Use boiled (then cooled) or other safe water if you have it (New York State Department of Health).
In a separate basin, mix 1 tablespoon (15 mL) of plain, unscented 5% to 9% bleach in each gallon (3.8 L) of water (New York State Department of Health; CDC for the strength).
Rinse or soak the washed dishes in it for 1 minute (New York State Department of Health, CDC).
Let them air dry completely before you use them. Don’t dry them with a towel (CDC, New York State Department of Health).

list: Clean counters and boards where food is made the same way: wash, rinse, the same bleach mix, air dry (CDC).
“Green” or “environmentally friendly” dishwasher additives are weak disinfectants; don’t rely on them alone (New York State Department of Health).
Dump dishwater as dirty wash water (see Garbage and dirty water).

blocks.p: Norovirus, a common cause of vomiting and diarrhea, can stay on surfaces for up to two weeks (University of Minnesota Extension). Clean up straight away (Minnesota Department of Health).

steps: Keep other people and pets away. Put on rubber or disposable gloves (CDC) and eye protection (CDC); a disposable apron and a mask as well if you have them (University of Minnesota Extension). Open windows and doors (CDC).

Soak up the vomit or stool with paper towels (CDC), or cover it with kitty litter or baking soda and scrape it up with cardboard or paper plates (University of Minnesota Extension). Never vacuum it (Minnesota Department of Health).
Put everything in a plastic trash bag (CDC).
Wash the whole area with soap and water (University of Minnesota Extension). The mess must be gone before you disinfect, or the disinfectant will not work (CDC).

Wet the whole area, well past the edge of the mess, with the strong mix: 1/3 cup (5 tablespoons, 75 mL) of plain, unscented 5% to 9% bleach in 1 gallon (3.8 L) of water (CDC). Use only bleach and water in your mixing bucket: nothing else. Keep it wet for 10 minutes if you can (CDC, evacuation centers), and never less than 5 minutes (CDC).
Clean the whole area again with soap and hot water (CDC).
Bag the cloths, apron and mask. Take your gloves off into the bag, seal it, and put on new gloves to carry it to a lidded trash can (University of Minnesota Extension).
Wash the soiled laundry (below), and wash your hands with soap and water (CDC).

list: Throw away food and food packaging within 25 feet (7.6 m) of the vomit or stool (University of Minnesota Extension). Keep the group’s food covered and stored away from where the sick person is, so there is less to lose (no source says this).
Keep people out of the room for 2 hours if you can; norovirus can stay in the air that long after someone vomits (University of Minnesota Extension).
Carpet or rugs: don’t vacuum first. Cover the spot with kitty litter or baking soda to soak it up (University of Minnesota Extension).

steps: Take off clothes and bedding with vomit or poop on them straight away. Wear rubber or disposable gloves (CDC).
Handle them carefully. Don’t shake them (CDC).
Remove any vomit or stool first, and keep these things apart from other laundry (University of Minnesota Extension).

With a machine: wash with detergent and hot water on the longest cycle, then dry on the highest heat (CDC). Household bleach can go in the rinse water (CDC, evacuation centers); follow the bleach label (University of Minnesota Extension).

Without a machine: keep your gloves on, use the warmest water you can, and dry everything completely (CDC). Household bleach can go in the rinse water (CDC, evacuation centers). Pour the wash water out as dirty wash water, well away from food and drinking water (see Garbage and dirty water).
Wash your hands with soap and water afterward (CDC).
